title: The smallest knotted ring in the diamond lattice
statement: A ring of atoms whose skeleton sits on the diamond lattice is a closed self-avoiding polygon of the lattice: distinct sites (integer points with all coordinates even and x + y + z = 0 mod 4, or all odd and x + y + z = 3 mod 4), each bonded to the next and the last to the first (squared distance 3), so that every bond angle is the tetrahedral angle, as in a cycloalkane in staggered conformations or a ring cut from diamond. How few atoms can a knotted ring have? The checker certifies the knot by its knot determinant |Delta(-1)|, computed from a regular projection, being larger than 1 (3 for the trefoil). The headline cell: find a knotted ring of fewer than 36 atoms (ours: a trefoil, knot determinant 3, with 36 atoms).
submission: Text file: the atoms of the ring in order, one line 'x y z' each: distinct sites of the diamond lattice, consecutive ones (and the last and the first) at squared distance 3.
score: the number of atoms of the ring (smaller is better), valid only when its knot determinant exceeds 1

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: a trefoil curve routed through the lattice and shortened by replacing windows of the ring with shorter lattice paths while it stays knotted, with random same-length moves between rounds; runs with five seeds all stopped at 36 atoms (tools/diamond_knot.py)

context: Knotted molecules were proposed by Frisch and Wasserman (1961) and first made by Dietrich-Buchecker and Sauvage (1989); how small a knotted ring can be is a basic question of chemical topology, since a tight knot strains every bond. On a lattice the question becomes exact: the minimal knotted polygons of the three cubic lattices are known, 24 edges in the simple cubic lattice (Diao 1993) and 15 and 18 edges in the face-centred and body-centred cubic lattices (Janse van Rensburg and Rechnitzer 2011), all trefoils. The diamond lattice is the lattice of chemistry: the carbon atoms of diamond, the backbone of an alkane or polyethylene chain in its staggered conformations (the rotational-isomeric-state lattice of polymer physics) and the oxygen atoms of cubic ice all sit on it, and every bond angle is tetrahedral. It is also the most open of these lattices, with four neighbours per site and no rings shorter than six, so its knots must be long. A ring is certified knotted when its knot determinant |Delta(-1)| (the determinant of the Fox colouring matrix of a diagram) exceeds 1; the checker computes it exactly from a regular projection. Our shortest ring is a trefoil of 36 atoms; whether a shorter knotted ring exists is open, and no lower bound beyond the trivial one is known to us.
references: H. L. Frisch, E. Wasserman, Chemical topology, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 83 (1961) 3789-3795
C. O. Dietrich-Buchecker, J.-P. Sauvage, A synthetic molecular trefoil knot, Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. Engl. 28 (1989) 189-192
Y. Diao, Minimal knotted polygons on the cubic lattice, J. Knot Theory Ramifications 2 (1993) 413-425
E. J. Janse van Rensburg, A. Rechnitzer, Minimal knotted polygons in cubic lattices, arXiv:1107.2162
R. H. Fox, A quick trip through knot theory, in: Topology of 3-Manifolds and Related Topics, Prentice-Hall, 1962, 120-167 (colourings and the knot determinant)

novelty.verdict: new question for the diamond lattice: minimal knotted polygons are known for the simple, face-centred and body-centred cubic lattices, but no minimal knotted ring of the diamond lattice was found, as far as our searches show.
closest: Minimal knotted polygons in the cubic lattices (Diao 1993; Janse van Rensburg and Rechnitzer, arXiv:1107.2162; upper bounds for cubic lattice knots, arXiv:1411.1849): the same question on the simple, face-centred and body-centred cubic lattices.

Knot probabilities of lattice polygons and ring polymers (Frisch-Wasserman-Delbruck conjecture; relative knot probabilities in confined lattice polygons, arXiv:2501.08835): statistics of long rings, not the smallest knot.
Synthetic molecular knots (Dietrich-Buchecker and Sauvage 1989 and later tight knots): real molecules, not a lattice extremum.
novelty.benchmark: no knot or lattice-polygon family in the benchmark

first_values.note: The diamond row is our shortest ring (refs/diamond-knot.txt), certified by the checker; the other rows are the published minima for comparison. The checker's knot determinant gives 3 for a trefoil curve, 5 for a figure-eight knot and 1 for an unknotted ring in our tests.

baseline.text: 36 atoms: a knotted ring of the diamond lattice with knot determinant 3, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026 (`refs/diamond-knot.txt`).
